pr_title: Prevent null ref in FeatureCollection access
pr_body:
If there is a race condition with Feature disposal (unawaited task or use after request end); it can pass the first Context Disposed check in `Fetch` and then null ref in `UpdateCached`

It should always throw Context Disposed rather than null ref

Seen in https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/25454
pr_comments:
@benaadams 5.0 is only taking high severity patches at this point. If we knew this would fix #25454 then we could ask for it, but I don't think we know enough about that issue yet. Can you retarget this to master please?

I do believe this addresses a race condition, but if #25454 were hitting this race condition then they would already be getting ObjectDisposedExceptions part of the time, right? Or is your assertion that these feature references could have been cached for a while so the app consistently hits the null ref issue?

> if #25454 were hitting this race condition then they would already be getting ObjectDisposedExceptions part of the time, right?

Might be something to ask about.

Will retarget

> If we want to guard against concurrent access, we should lock, but I don't think it's worth it. I'm fine with null-checking at the beginning of Fetch like we already do, but repeatedly null-checking Collection is overly defensive in my opinion.

Probably fair. 

Related https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/26128
Ah no, not related, more likely use after free rather than concurrent access
@benaadams @pranavkm @Tratcher Are there any objections to closing this?

issue_context.title: DefaultHttpResponse throws null ref when trying to access Cookies, even when using null check, only from bots
issue_context.body:
### Describe the bug
I'm attempting to set a cookie with the following code ([source is here](https://github.com/POPWorldMedia/POPForums/blob/f52c9a99d1090bb1ff1b776be9f3ea253ab7eb91/src/PopForums.Mvc/Areas/Forums/Services/TopicViewCountService.cs#L39)):
```
var context = _httpContextAccessor.HttpContext;
context.Response?.Cookies?.Append(CookieKey, topic.TopicID.ToString());
```
...where the context accessor is inserted via DI. However, per the stack trace listed below, `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.DefaultHttpResponse.get_Cookies()` throws a null ref exception. What's even more strange is that it only occurs with search indexing bots. So far I've logged errors from Bing, Google, webmeup, brandwatch, mj12bot, semrush, grapeshot and others. It's __always__ a bot.

My assumption is that even if the `Cookies` property in my code was null, it shouldn't fail, and stack trace is throwing from within the `DefaultHttpResponse` code. Two interesting points though:
* It's always a bot when this error is logged.
* It seems to have started when I migrated the site to a Linux app service on Azure (was previously a Windows based app service on Azure).

### To Reproduce

review_comments: Why is this and the above line using and null-checking `Collection` instead of using `collection`?

`collection` will be live (has passed null check) and not reflect whether the Context has been disposed; so will for example update Kestrel's feature collection for the next request rather than the "current" one.
Its already passed a null check in `Fetch` before calling this so `Collection` gets nulled between the two calls

Like you said in [your comment](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/25454#issuecomment-686154020) on the issue, "this would mean the Context/Request/Response is disposed while the `Fetch` method is still accessed and the request is finished while it is still active, so concurrent activity; most likely from a missed `await`." That basically means all bets are off unless we start locking.

I don't want perfect to be the enemy of good. I totally support throwing ODEs instead of NREs where we can, but this change allows `Fetch` to complete without throwing in situations it should throw and would throw today. We could be setting the `cached` item one `Collection` (or not set anything at all because it's null), but using the `Revision` of the next `Collection`. Today, if Collection is null when we try to set the cached item in the `Collection`, we'd throw an NRE instead of leaving `FeatureReferences` in an inconsistent state.

If we use `collection` instead of `Collection` here, at least the `FeatureReferences` stays in a consistent state. Sure, it could update the next request instead of the current one, but that's a real possibility with or without this change.

>  this change allows `Fetch` to complete without throwing in situations it should throw and would throw today. 

It just changes it to throw ODE rather than NRE; using `collection` rather than `Collection` would allow it to succeed as `FeatureReferences` is a struct which is "disposed" by being set to `default`
https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/e0467560e11a739897521326b543e9652a4edb77/src/Http/Http/src/Internal/DefaultHttpResponse.cs#L40-L43

Using `Collection` means it picks up that its been nulled; whereas using `collection` would mean it writes through ignoring that its been disposed and disconnected?

> If you are talking about skipping the null in the set and then passing as not null in the revision, that's a pretty small window

That is what I'm talking about. Given there's already a null check in `Fetch`, this entire race is a pretty small window. That doesn't mean it won't happen.

If it used `collection` then it wouldn't check for null again and everything would complete (albeit on the newer request); so it would reduce the chance of it throwing?

As it currently is it's more likely to throw a ODE than not throw? (in this narrow corner case)

It just now won't throw a NRE

With this change, it's less likely to throw than before even when it should. By using `collection`, it would even be less likely to throw than with this change, but at least it wouldn't be getting a `Revision` from the new collection and allow the next call to `Fetch` to return a cached value that hasn't actually been set.

> but at least it wouldn't be getting a `Revision` from the new collection and allow the next call to `Fetch` to return a cached value that hasn't actually been set.

On Kestrel the collection is the same; there isn't a new collection so it's going to return the same value for `Revision` regardless; so its better if it throws?

Kestrel won't return the same value for Revision. 

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/63116086f0098a7a8f2c5196d9fa778bc3df3b23/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/Http/HttpProtocol.Generated.cs#L83-L88

My main objection isn't about any particular race condition being made better or worse though. I simply think this is too clever.

If we want to guard against concurrent access, we should lock, but I don't think it's worth it. I'm fine with null-checking at the beginning of Fetch like we already do, but repeatedly null-checking Collection is overly defensive in my opinion.
